line: Our theories were nearer the measured number than readers with no theory in 190 of 394 predictions: no better.

theories.name: Self-copying circuits
theories.statement: The base's loops and cap hits come from early-to-mid-layer circuits that copy its own earlier text; RL's cap-hit gain weakens that pathway in layers 0-15.
theories.why: A forecaster given this theory was nearer than reader 1 on 21 of the 58 held-out numbers and farther on 14; against reader 2, 19 and 17. A planted theory with every effect reversed scored the same, so no theory beat the readers.

theories.name: Token-budget controller
theories.statement: RL's lead is a learned token-budget controller, trained because 3.1 scores truncated rollouts as failures; it is not new math skill.
theories.why: A forecaster given this theory was nearer than reader 1 on 23 of the 58 held-out numbers and farther on 17; against reader 2, 22 and 20. A planted theory with every effect reversed scored the same, so no theory beat the readers.

theories.name: Base decays as text grows
theories.statement: The cued base has RL's per-step skill; the gap is the base degrading as its own long solution grows, which RL repaired by training truncated rollouts as failures.
theories.why: A forecaster given this theory was nearer than reader 1 on 24 of the 58 held-out numbers and farther on 17; against reader 2, 18 and 15. A planted theory with every effect reversed scored the same, so no theory beat the readers.

theories.name: One answer-mode switch
theories.statement: Most of the RL gain is one answer-mode switch (deliberate, box the answer, stop), stored redundantly along a diffuse direction, so any small unbiased fraction of the delta flips it.
theories.why: A forecaster given this theory was nearer than reader 1 on 22 of the 58 held-out numbers and farther on 20; against reader 2, 18 and 21. A planted theory with every effect reversed scored the same, so no theory beat the readers.

theories.name: Deliberation and stopping
theories.statement: The gain is a general deliberation shift that the cue, Code-RL and 3.0 share, plus stopping calibration that only 3.1 learned; the cued-base gap is the second part.
theories.why: A forecaster given this theory was nearer than reader 1 on 21 of the 58 held-out numbers and farther on 21; against reader 2, 16 and 24. A planted theory with every effect reversed scored the same, so no theory beat the readers.

theories.name: Only low-rank part works
theories.statement: The working part of the weight change is low-rank and near-linear; the high-rank remainder, which holds most of its energy, is optimizer noise.
theories.why: A forecaster given this theory was nearer than reader 1 on 15 of the 58 held-out numbers and farther on 22; against reader 2, 17 and 22. A planted theory with every effect reversed scored the same, so no theory beat the readers.

theories.name: Self-copying circuits
theories.statement: The base's loops and cap hits come from early-to-mid-layer circuits that copy its own earlier text; RL's cap-hit gain weakens that pathway in layers 0-15.

theories.name: Token-budget controller

theories.why: Round 2 score: 1 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 16 claims.

theories.name: Base decays as text grows
theories.statement: The cued base has RL's per-step skill; the gap is the base degrading as its own long solution grows, which RL repaired by training truncated rollouts as failures.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 2 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 12 claims.

theories.name: One answer-mode switch
theories.statement: Most of the RL gain is one answer-mode switch (deliberate, box the answer, stop), stored redundantly along a diffuse direction, so any small unbiased fraction of the delta flips it.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 3 wins and 2 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 13 claims.

theories.name: Deliberation and stopping
theories.statement: The gain is a general deliberation shift that the cue, Code-RL and 3.0 share, plus stopping calibration that only 3.1 learned; the cued-base gap is the second part.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 0 wins and 0 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 8 claims.

theories.name: Only low-rank part works
theories.statement: The working part of the weight change is low-rank and near-linear; the high-rank remainder, which holds most of its energy, is optimizer noise.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 3 wins and 2 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 19 claims.

theories.name: Entropy drops at forks
theories.statement: The weight change lowers next-token entropy only at the base's high-entropy fork tokens, so RL ignores temperature while the base loops when cooled and errs when heated.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 1 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 6 claims.

theories.name: Sign pattern carries it
theories.statement: The delta's effect sits in its coherent sign pattern, with hundreds to thousands of times a random direction's Fisher curvature; DARE fails near keep 0.01-0.05 %.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 3 wins and 2 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 15 claims.
theories.review: weak: the three wins follow from a saturating dose curve without leverage or signs, the claims about leverage and signs for these models are already in 2610.37719, and the theory's own inferences fail on the counter-examples it chose (Code-RL 450/390 against its 412/245; word salad rising to 34/500 at a = 1.5). Only the DARE-cliff and sign-only predictions are left to test.

theories.name: High-curvature signs
theories.statement: The delta acts through coherent signs along high-curvature directions, about 700 times a random direction; unbiased resampling keeps the gain, random signs remove it, SFT deltas break.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 0 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 5 claims.

theories.name: Surprise sets accuracy
theories.statement: Base accuracy at a sampler setting depends on the per-token surprise of its text (too low: loops; too high: drift); the cue lowers entropy, so truncation hurts the cued base.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 2 wins and 0 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 8 claims.
theories.review: No team result refutes it by its own thresholds, but its two wins are explained as well by noise (t51) and by a grader format artefact (t09, which also explains its t10 miss); its loop half is published (2007.14966, 2512.12895, 2610.24715) and its entropy-to-optimal-temperature half is published across models (2502.05234), leaving only the untested prompt-level sign flip of top-p (plain base at T 1.0 / top-p 0.95) a…

theories.name: 700 times a random edit
theories.statement: The delta moves output 700 times more per unit energy than a random direction; DARE holds to keep 0.1 % and collapses near 0.01 %; random weight noise reduces loops.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 1 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 5 claims.

theories.name: Per-position temperature
theories.statement: One global temperature acts on two kinds of positions: low temperature starts loops at rare fork tokens, high temperature causes slips elsewhere; a per-position temperature would fix the base.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 1 wins and 2 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 6 claims.

theories.name: Many small sign entries
theories.statement: Accuracy is carried by the dense sign pattern of many small entries; an edit recovers accuracy in proportion to the share of it kept; Code-RL gives no math gain.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 1 wins and 0 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 10 claims.

theories.name: Weak base error detector
theories.statement: The cued base's gap is a weak error detector, not weaker per-step math: RL notices and re-derives errors more often, so a 4-sample vote closes about half the base's gap.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 0 wins and 0 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 2 claims.

theories.name: Loops, slips on one axis
theories.statement: Loops and slips are two ends of one axis, the per-token surprise of sampled text; the cue lowers entropy, RL sits far from both ends, and raising surprise cuts loops.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 0 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 4 claims.

theories.name: Task lives in the signs
theories.statement: The base and optimizer set which entries move, and how far; the task is written only in the signs, which act on any math text and leave general text alone.
theories.why: Round 2 score: 0 wins and 1 losses on the claims where both readers' numbers lay outside its interval, of 9 claims.

theories.name: One answer-mode switch
theories.statement: Most of the RL gain is one answer-mode switch (deliberate, box the answer, stop), stored redundantly along a diffuse direction, so any small unbiased fraction of the delta flips it.
theories.why: Round 3 score: +2.62 nats against the readers over 12 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Only low-rank part works
theories.statement: The working part of the weight change is low-rank and near-linear; the high-rank remainder, which holds most of its energy, is optimizer noise.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -4.60 nats against the readers over 8 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Sign pattern carries it
theories.statement: The delta's effect sits in its coherent sign pattern, with hundreds to thousands of times a random direction's Fisher curvature; DARE fails near keep 0.01-0.05 %.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -3.20 nats against the readers over 7 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Surprise sets accuracy
theories.statement: Base accuracy at a sampler setting depends on the per-token surprise of its text (too low: loops; too high: drift); the cue lowers entropy, so truncation hurts the cued base.
theories.why: Round 3 score: +0.00 nats against the readers over 0 claims.

theories.name: General plus math part
theories.statement: The RL delta has a general reliability part, shared with Code-RL and saturated at a = 0.25, and a dose-growing math part needed only on problems the base rarely solves.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -0.35 nats against the readers over 6 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Tail tokens end loops
theories.statement: The cued base leaves loops only through low-probability tail tokens that T < 1 and truncation delete; RL adds a constant push toward probable 'Wait'/'Hmm', so it ignores temperature.
theories.why: Round 3 score: +0.67 nats against the readers over 1 claims.
theories.review: weak: its single winning claim (t13, +0.67 nats) comes from the 'constant push' reading that was already on the board and that the reversal shared, not from the tail-escape mechanism. The loop-locking half is published (2610.24715), the core predictions (P1, P2 and the offline hold-on ratios) are untested, and result-6de887 shows T 0.6 loops can be cut by neuron ablation with no accuracy gain.

theories.name: Two stopping habits
theories.statement: RL's gain over the cued base is two stopping habits: a general commit-and-box habit (Code-RL shares it, a = 0.25 holds it) and a math-specific check-before-stopping habit for long problems.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -2.67 nats against the readers over 4 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Spread at progress steps
theories.statement: On hard problems the base spreads probability at progress steps; low temperature turns the spread into self-reinforcing loops, T 1.0 into wrong turns; RL is concentrated, so temperature barely matters.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -1.36 nats against the readers over 3 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Truncation causes repeats
theories.statement: Over-truncated sampling sends a pretrained-style policy into repetition basins; 3.1, trained at exact T 1.0 with truncated rollouts as negatives, suppressed them, so 3.1 ignores temperature and 3.0 does not.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -1.43 nats against the readers over 2 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Sharpening, then late part
theories.statement: The delta is an early sharpening part, overshot several-fold and fully expressed at a = 0.25, plus a late part, growing with a, that solves what the base rarely solves.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -7.95 nats against the readers over 11 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Deliberate, then commit
theories.statement: The RL-Zero gain is a general 'deliberate, then commit' part (every RL-Zero delta has it, saturated at a = 0.25, replaceable by the cue) plus a math-specific part linear in a.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -2.69 nats against the readers over 11 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Loops open at impasses
theories.statement: A loop is an absorbing hazard that opens at impasses; T 0.6 traps finishable medium-length solutions, while at T >= 1 only fixed long, mostly lost problems loop.
theories.why: Round 3 score: +0.00 nats against the readers over 0 claims.

theories.name: Tail tokens derail steps
theories.statement: The cued base's T 1.0 deficit is low-probability tail tokens that derail steps, adding up with length; RL shrinks the tail; label-free tail cuts also remove loop escapes, netting zero.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -0.24 nats against the readers over 4 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: Shared low-dose stop gate
theories.statement: Any outcome-reward RL delta has a shared low-dose part gating settle, verify and stop (saturated at a = 0.25) and a math-specific part paying only on long, hard problems.
theories.why: Round 3 score: -4.35 nats against the readers over 11 claims (90 % interval reaches 0).

theories.name: f2-m01
theories.statement: The autobench agent works under a fixed generation time per experiment, so it buys votes by shortening each sample (its best config: 10 samples at about 1,100 tokens each). Most MATH-500 problems are solved in under 2,000 tokens, so short samples plus a vote score well on dev100, but hard328 solutions need 6,000-14,000 tokens and short samples never reach them. For the base, each doubling of the token budget past 8,000 buys fewer problems.
theories.why: 1 of its forecasts measured so far, 0 inside its interval, -3.00 nats against the two readers.

theories.name: f2-m02
theories.statement: The cued base's wrong answers on a problem rarely share a value: slips are per-sample chance events that land on scattered numbers, while right answers coincide. A plurality vote therefore wins a problem once the right share exceeds the largest wrong-value share, far below one half, and keeps converting such problems as samples are added, with no plateau by 12. The loss is in ties, which odd sample counts and more samples dissolve.
theories.why: 1 of its forecasts measured so far, 1 inside its interval, +0.38 nats against the two readers.

theories.name: f2-m03
theories.statement: The top singular directions of the RL-Math difference set when the base stops, not whether its reasoning is right: their dose sets the cap-hit rate, while right answers per finished answer stay near the base's 0.65; RL's correctness lives in the remainder of the difference. Past dose 1, extra finishes on problems the base cannot solve are guesses, so accuracy is flat from 1x to 2x, and on MATH-500, with few cap hits, the dial adds little.
theories.why: 3 of its forecasts measured so far, 0 inside its interval, -7.07 nats against the two readers.

theories.name: f2-m04
theories.statement: A capped sample gives no answer, so in a plurality vote it abstains instead of adding a wrong value. Think-SFT's vote sits near its pass@4 because its unsolved samples run to the cap rather than box a guess. Anything that makes it finish, a 32k cap or the RL difference, turns abstentions into mostly wrong, scattered answers that tie or outvote lone right samples: single scores rise, vote gains shrink.
theories.why: 1 of its forecasts measured so far, 1 inside its interval, +0.31 nats against the two readers.

theories.name: f2-m05
theories.statement: The RL-Math difference carries RL's habit of ending a long unsolved attempt with an asserted, underived number (per 1,312 hard328 samples RL finishes long and wrong 381 times, the base 281). Added to another model it turns unfinished attempts into such guesses and cuts slower derivations short. On new problems, where RL's finished precision is 43 %, the guesses are wrong, so gains measured on hard328 shrink or reverse; on MATH-500 it is neutral.
theories.why: 3 of its forecasts measured so far, 1 inside its interval, -5.88 nats against the two readers.

theories.name: f2-m06
theories.statement: Think-SFT's difference from the base carries long derivation; the RL-Math difference carries a controller that stops once an answer is derived. The two are orthogonal (cosine -0.00001), so their sum acts as both, but inside Think-SFT's long traces the controller is diluted and needs a = 2 to reach RL's stopping strength. At a = 2 the model derives like Think-SFT and finishes like RL on any set and seed, so gains are largest where Think-SFT caps most.
